Hey,

I want to ask for your opinion if Mathlib is a good place to hold such a theory. A lot of research has been done to find mathematical theories that have the same proof strength as popular complexity classes. So, you have mathematical theories in which it's not provable that for any sequence, the sorted(sequence) exists - but with enough strength, you can prove that every number n has its prime_factorization(n). The field is bounded arithmetic and is like the extreme case of reverse mathematics.

What's nice about it are two things:

  • the field doesn't have the invisible maths problem that emerges naturally when trying to un-handwave the proofs from complexity theory. The field is susceptible to being formalized and I have some work on that.
  • the style of reasoning is different to imperative programming, but it's not unnatural - in Implicit Computational Complexity, people studied other ways to capture complexity classes and they all fall into 'unusable' bucket for now, due to just how hugely different their paradigm is
  • difficult results have been obtained inside of these weak theories already, so there are a few difficult algorithms that could have their complexity proven: e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12011

Do you think we could host another top-level theory in Mathlib? Such as Mathlib.BoundedArithmetic, probably using some tooling from Mathlib.ModelTheory (for syntax of logic). There surely be a problem with finding reviewers in that field for now I think, as that theory is rather niche?

I attach a screenshot from Logical Foundations of Proof Complexity (2010; Cook, Nguyen) that gives a hint of how the theory hierarchy looks like and the theorems that correspond
Also, a presentation I gave last year at AITP2025 about my shot at formalizing these results: https://ruplet.com/aitp-presentation.pdf
No, you should create your own library. Trying to put this into Mathlib would only lead to frustration, with zero reviewers for you PRs.
